https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A Board of Education presentation titled 'Exploring Our Data Story,' delivered November 19, 2024, reviewing how Troy School District uses summative and formative assessment data within its MTSS framework. It covers M-STEP (grades 3-7), PSAT 8, SAT 11, AP, and classroom measures such as Fountas & Pinnell, Bridges Math, Common Lit, and NWEA. Highlights include International Academy East IB diploma acquisition of 81% in 2024, AP Honor Roll status (Troy High Gold, Athens High advancing to Gold), 42% of 11th graders in AP English in 2024, and more than 290 Class of 2024 CTE completers.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A district Student Achievement presentation, 'Exploring Our Data Story,' for the November 19, 2024 Board of Education meeting.

Framework
- Summative measures: M-STEP (Gr 3-7), PSAT 8 / SAT 11, College Board AP; Exit data: TCCHS graduation rate.
- Formative measures: Fountas & Pinnell (K-5), Bridges Math (K-5), Common Lit (ELA 6-12), NWEA Math (6-Alg 1).
- Data used within the district's MTSS process, including a partnership with NSK12 on ELD and Special Education supports.

Selected results
- International Academy East IB Diploma acquisition: 81% (2024), 72% (2023), 88% (2022), 87% (2021), 90% (2020), 82% (2019).
- AP Honor Roll: Troy High School Gold in 2022-23 and 2023-24; Athens High School Silver then Gold.
- AP 11th-grade English enrollment: 402 of 948 (42%) in 2024, up from 34% in 2023.
- Seal of Biliteracy: 15 in 2024, projected 18 in 2025.
- CTE: more than 290 Class of 2024 students earned completer status.

Purpose
Show how assessment data informs instruction, MTSS decision-making, and district improvement, and to celebrate outcomes.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Titled 'Exploring Our Data Story,' this presentation was delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on November 19, 2024. Its objectives were to review district goals, provide context to enhance understanding of data, and share how data is used to drive district systems and processes.

The presentation distinguishes summative from formative assessment. District-level summative measures include M-STEP (grades 3-7), PSAT 8 and SAT 11, and College Board Advanced Placement; the stated exit measure is the TCCHS (Troy graduation) rate. Classroom-level formative measures include Fountas & Pinnell (K-5), Bridges Math (K-5), Common Lit (ELA 6-12), and NWEA Math (grade 6 through Algebra 1). It notes the value of summative data for cohort tracking and cross-district comparison while acknowledging granularity limitations. Several slides present county comparisons alongside Free/Reduced Lunch (FRL) rates for ELA and Math M-STEP (grades 3-7) and middle-school M-STEP for grades 6 and 7, plus PSAT 8 (EBRW and Math, including an Oakland Schools LEA average versus TSD comparison) and SAT 11 (EBRW, Math, and overall).

Data use is framed within the Multi-Tiered System of Supports (MTSS) process, emphasizing collaboration, ongoing adjustments, and a partnership with NSK12 to evaluate supports for students receiving ELD, Special Education, and other services. Focus areas include access to Tier 1 core instruction, access to content-strong staff, additional learning time, and ongoing professional learning (citing an October 31-November 1 'Trailguide'). Formative slides cover Fountas & Pinnell and math benchmarks by grade, a new NWEA universal screener for middle-school mathematics (enabling participation in a third-party study with Illustrative Mathematics), and Common Lit assessment reporting.

Celebrated outcomes are specific. International Academy East IB Diploma acquisition rates were 81% (2024), 72% (2023), 88% (2022), 87% (2021), 90% (2020), and 82% (2019). On the AP School Honor Roll, Athens High School moved from Silver (2022-23) to Gold (2023-24) -- College Culture rising from 61% (232/378) to 70% (253/362), College Credit from 50% (189/378) to 58% (209/362), and College Optimization from 27% (102/378) to 23% (83/362); Troy High School held Gold both years -- College Culture 69% (364/527) to 75% (381/510), College Credit 65% (341/527) to 67% (341/510), and College Optimization 30% (158/527) to 30% (153/510). https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Minutes of the regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education held October 15, 2024 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. All seven board members were present: Schmidt, Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson. Superintendent Machesky attended with administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Foren, and Trudel, before an audience of approximately 25 people.

Recognitions and Mission Moment: The board's Student Spotlight honored Athens High School senior Maisie Justes for her achievements as a filmmaker in the TSD Creative Guild; Thomas Butcher introduced her. The meeting's Mission Moment recognized Learning Disabilities Awareness Month. Additional recognitions listed were Principal Appreciation Month, the 2024 National School Public Relations Association (NSPRA) Awards, and the 2025 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists.

Resolution -- Learning Disabilities Month (October 2024): Moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Dr. Philippart, the resolution recites that learning disabilities refer to differences in how brains work, which may affect the acquisition, organization, retention, understanding, or use of verbal or nonverbal information; that they range in severity and may impact oral language, reading, written language, and mathematics; that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability; that such disabilities may co-exist with other conditions and can affect individuals regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, or other intersecting factors; and that, with appropriate supports and services, individuals with learning disabilities can achieve their goals and participate fully in society. The resolution joins Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2024 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. It was adopted by a vote of 7 Yes, 0 No (Resolution Adopted).

Resolution -- Principal Appreciation Month: Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mr. Haupt, this resolution commends the district's elementary and secondary principals, reciting that energetic and inspiring school leadership is essential to ensuring all Troy students are college and career ready and that K-12 principals act as a vital liaison between the school and the community it serves. The extracted text is truncated before the vote on this resolution is recorded and does not include the meeting's consent agenda or later business.

- PSAT/SAT: TSD exceeds Oakland Schools and the state in EBRW and Math every reported year. 2023-24 SAT: TSD EBRW 77.3%, Math 59.5% (state about 51.3% / 26.3%). 2023-24 PSAT 8: TSD EBRW about 84%, Math about 64%.

- IB (International Academy East) diploma acquisition: 81% (2024), 72% (2023), 88% (2022), 87% (2021), 90% (2020).
- AP 11 ELA enrollment rose to 42% of 11th graders (402 of 948) in 2024.

Systems / next steps: MTSS decision-making; a new NWEA universal screener for middle-school math (enabling an Illustrative Mathematics third-party study); a partnership with NSK12 on ELD and Special Education supports; and focus on Tier 1 core instruction, content-strong staff, added learning time, and professional learning.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Board of Education presentation titled "Exploring Our Data Story," delivered at the November 19, 2024 meeting, reviewing Troy School District student-achievement data and how the district uses it. Stated objectives were to review district goals, provide context to enhance understanding of the data, and share how data drives district systems and processes.

Assessment framework: The presentation distinguishes summative, district-level assessments -- M-STEP (grades 3-7), PSAT 8 / SAT 11, and College Board Advanced Placement -- from formative, classroom-level tools: Fountas & Pinnell benchmark (K-5), Bridges Math (K-5), CommonLit (ELA 6-12), and NWEA Math (grade 6 through Algebra 1), plus exit data, the Troy Career Center High School (TCCHS) graduation rate, and early-childhood enrollment. It notes limitations of summative data (useful for cohort tracking and cross-district comparison but lacking granularity for specific performance insights).

PSAT/SAT results (percent meeting or exceeding expectations, TSD vs. Oakland Schools vs. state): TSD consistently outperforms both benchmarks. On PSAT 8 Evidence-Based Reading & Writing (EBRW), TSD scored in the low-to-mid 80s (84.2 in 2023-24) versus Oakland Schools in the high-60s to low-70s and the state near 60. On PSAT 8 Math, TSD ranged from about 75.1 (2018-19) to 64.3 (2023-24), well above Oakland Schools (about 42-53) and the state (about 33-41). On SAT 11 EBRW, TSD posted 82.9, 75.3, 76.9, and 77.3 across 2018-19 through 2023-24 (state about 51-55); on SAT Math, TSD posted 73.6, 61.6, 61.3, and 59.5 (state about 26-36). TSD's SAT overall rate (meeting expectations in both Math and EBRW) was roughly 57-70%, far above Oakland Schools and the state.

Advanced Placement: Both comprehensive high schools earned College Board AP Honor Roll recognition. Troy High School was rated Gold in both 2023-24 and 2022-23; Athens High School was Gold (2023-24) and Silver (2022-23). "School Overall" AP participation was 75% (381/510) at Troy and 70% (253/362) at Athens in 2023-24. College Culture (took any AP exam) reached 67% at Troy and 58% at Athens; College Credit (scored 3 or higher) was 30% at Troy and 23% at Athens. AP 11 ELA enrollment rose to 42% of 11th graders (402 of 948) in 2024, up from 34% (315 of 932) in 2023.

International Baccalaureate: International Academy East IB diploma acquisition rates were 82% (2019), 90% (2020), 87% (2021), 88% (2022), 72% (2023), and 81% (2024).

Systems and next steps: The district frames data use within its Multi-Tiered System of Supports (MTSS), emphasizing access to Tier 1 core instruction for all students, content-strong staff, additional learning time, and ongoing professional learning (citing an October 31 and November 1 "Trailguide" event). It describes a partnership with NSK12 to evaluate supports and structures for students receiving services in English Language Development (ELD), Special Education, and other areas, and reports establishing a universal NWEA screener for middle-school mathematics, which middle-school math specialists use to identify students needing further diagnostic assessment and which allows the district to participate in a third-party study with Illustrative Mathematics. Formative tools such as CommonLit are used to set baselines, identify students needing immediate support, drive whole-class and small-group instruction, monitor growth over time, and support student goal-setting. Identified district improvement needs include better screening and diagnostics for the MTSS process, forming work groups to build capacity, and shared ownership of the MTSS process. The presentation closes by celebrating the district's investment in early childhood.

Business Services Update titled General Fund Amendment 1, presented at the Troy School District Board of Education workshop on December 3, 2024. The presentation first explains school funding for 2024-25. The total foundation allowance is $10,394 per pupil, composed of a state-provided portion plus locally levied millage: a Non-Homestead levy equal to $2,804 per pupil and a Hold-Harmless (Homestead) levy equal to $786 per pupil. A five-year breakdown shows the state share climbing from $6,251 (2020-21) to $6,523, $6,733, $6,971, and $6,804 (2024-25); the non-homestead local share rising from $2,030 to $2,121, $2,355, $2,637, and $2,804; and the hold-harmless share moving from $1,034 to $786 and holding at $786. Historical total foundation figures of $9,315, $9,430, and $9,874 are shown for earlier years, reaching $10,394 for the current year.

A central message is that the district's $10,394 foundation allowance is $4,236 per pupil less than the inflation-adjusted foundation allowance, a gap the presentation quantifies as approximately $51.9 million in lower revenue for the Troy School District this school year. It also notes that $3,590 of the allowance is dependent upon voter approval.

General Fund Amendment 1 revenue adjustments represent a 0.5% increase from the June budget. Drivers include a foundation allowance of $10,394 on 12,260 FTE (a decrease of 100 students); Section 74b Clean Bus funding (+$823k); Section 22b discretionary funding ($740k); MPSERS Section 147a(4) (+$5.05 million); Section 23g Back on Track (+$452k); and Section 31aa Mental Health carryover (+$2.70 million). These are partially offset by reductions: Section 147c(1) UAAL (-$7.82 million), Section 20f Hold Harmless Guarantee (-$1.47 million), Education Comp (-$637k), and Section 97 Security (-$745k).

Amendment 1 expenditure adjustments represent a 0.3% decrease from June. Salaries and benefits are adjusted for current staffing and lane adjustments; benefits are further adjusted for the Section 147c retirement-revenue increase; and adjustments are made to debt service and to capital outlay for GASB 87 leases. The presentation closes with a questions slide. Overall, it documents the first formal General Fund budget amendment of the 2024-25 fiscal year and situates it within the state's foundation-allowance funding structure.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Troy School District Accountability Plan, presented at the Board of Education workshop on December 3, 2024. The plan is organized around the district's World Class for All strategic pillars, each with objectives, key results, December 2024 celebrations, and challenges/recommendations.

Green Pillar - Early Childhood to Career: Objectives include continuing to invest in high-quality early childhood education and advocating for universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds; expanding college and career pathways for middle and high school students through high-quality career and technical education (CTE) that connects underrepresented students to in-demand careers via partnerships with colleges, employers, and stakeholders (work-based learning, credential earning, and college credit); and building a consistent K-12 career readiness plan. Key results and celebrations include increasing GSRP preschool slots from 98 to 160; the Portrait of a Learner initiative; the Section 99b Computer Science/Computational Thinking grant and K-12 CS alignment with Oakland Schools and MDE; expanded maker-centered learning spaces reaching the high school; Early Middle College with LTU (Lawrence Technological University); a Business Round Table; growing the Career Accelerator Program to 60 students; 8th-grade interviews and portfolios integrated with middle school Celebrations of Learning; and Athens being named one of two schools in the state to pilot the Ignite Program (Mechatronics). More than 290 students from the class of 2024 earned completer status in CTE courses spanning Education, Radio and Television Broadcasting, Marketing, Finance, Drafting and Design Technology, Cooking and Culinary Arts, Automotive Technician, Computer Programming, Mechatronics, Business, and Woodworking. Challenges include the transition to a 5-Day Model, preparation for Universal Preschool, prioritizing digital citizenship K-12, growing computer science in the K-12 curriculum, and shifting from electives to CTE programs.

Red Pillar - Equity and Well-Being: Objectives emphasize equity and well-being, funding investments to support the whole child, and an elevated focus on Alignment, Access, and Agency district-wide. Key results include an SEL curriculum pilot and SEL-focused programming K-12 (more than 1,600 SEL lessons in Everyday Speech used September through November); Behavioral Threat Assessment (BTA) and Suicide Risk Assessment committee work, including NTAC adoption and continued partnership with Margaret Coggins and the BTA Team; suicide-awareness professional learning (Winter 2024); Elevating Student Experience efforts such as Belonging Focus Group sessions and Student Equity Council expansion; Family and Community Engagement through the Community Book Read and Continuing the Conversation Series; and Restorative Culture and Community, with all building teams trained as of November 2024. Belonging is described as a continuing North Star.

Blue Pillar - Deep Learning: Objectives include creating and sustaining systems of support at all levels through MTSS to deepen learning and empower student voice; improving technology access for students and families with quality training; pursuing global best practices across content areas (NPDL, the 6 C's, learning partnerships); and assessing and acting on the need for upgraded facilities. Highlighted work includes a furniture pilot with 36 teachers K-12, playground redesign informed by student designs and input (with quoted student feedback about places to climb, movable seating, and shaded outdoor spaces), a focus on professional learning communities and Universal Design and MTSS at the secondary level, and continued attention to learning environments coordinated with the district's bond initiatives.

A “Business Services Update — General Fund Amendment 1” presentation dated December 3, 2024, prepared for a Troy Board of Education workshop to explain the first amendment to the district’s 2024-25 General Fund budget and to provide context on Michigan school funding.

Understanding school funding (2024-25): A district’s foundation allowance is built from the state foundation allowance plus other revenue sources (sales, income, use, liquor, excise, cigarette, and lottery taxes), with local levies layered on. For Troy, the hold-harmless (homestead) levy equals $786 per pupil and the non-homestead levy equals $2,804 per pupil. The presentation charts the foundation allowance breakdown from 2020-21 through 2024-25, with the state portion at $6,251, $6,523, $6,733, $6,971, and $6,804; the local non-homestead portion at $2,030, $2,121, $2,355, $2,637, and $2,804; and the hold-harmless (homestead) portion at $1,034, $786, $786, $786, and $786 — yielding totals of $9,315, $9,430, $9,874, $10,394, and $10,394. An amount of $3,590 is noted as dependent upon voter approval. For 2024-25, the foundation allowance of $10,394 is $4,236 per pupil less than the inflation-adjusted foundation allowance, a deficit that equates to approximately $51.9 million in lower revenue for the Troy School District this school year.

Amendment 1 revenue adjustments (a 0.5% increase from the June budget): the FTE count is set at 12,260 (down 100) with the $10,394 foundation; increases include 74b Clean Bus (+$823k), 22b Discretionary ($740k), MPSERS 147a(4) (+$5.05M), 23g Back on Track (+$452k), and 31aa Mental Health Carryover (+$2.70M); decreases include 147c(1) UAAL (-$7.82M), 20f Hold Harmless Guarantee (-$1.47M), Education Comp (-$637k), and Section 97 Security (-$745k).

Amendment 1 expenditure adjustments (a 0.3% decrease from June): salaries and benefits are adjusted for current staffing and lane adjustments; benefits are adjusted for the 147c retirement revenue increase; and debt service and capital outlay (GASB 87 leases) are also addressed. The presentation closes with a Questions slide.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presentation to the Troy Board of Education dated December 17, 2024 (titled 'Attendance Area Review, District School Troy') providing an update on the district's Attendance Area Review Committee (AARC).

Background points: attendance-area reviews are described as common practice conducted every 5-10 years, with previous AARC groups in 2015 and 2018 and a Facilities Review Committee in 2022 comprising 62 members. The current effort is a roughly six-month process incorporating staff, student, cabinet, and board of education feedback. Drivers cited include a double split at Troy Union and additional elementary single splits, current ratios at each middle school, enrollment projections, birth rate, and schools-of-choice (SOC). The presentation notes that the new Smith Middle School is built for 750/800 students; that Boulan Park will move to Smith during renovation, followed by Larson Middle School; and that all four middle schools rank in the top 6 in Michigan per NICHE/Metro Parent rankings.

The AARC has three stated goals: Goal 1, right-size the middle schools with equal student ratios; Goal 2, resolve double splits; and Goal 3, no impact on the high school. The district hired Plante Moran to help study options.

The work is organized into four phases:
- Phase 1: Discovery (the current phase) - the committee was formed and research, analysis, and planning commence; the committee develops potential recommendations.
- Phase 2: Recommendation (January) - the committee provides the board with a recommendation (options), and the board determines whether the district should move forward.
- Phase 3: Feedback (February-April) - the district will hold four listening sessions for all families, one at each middle school, and send out a community survey for additional feedback.
- Phase 4: Determination (April/May) - the district will provide the board with a summary of feedback, and the board will determine any future changes.

Next steps are listed as: February/March community meetings at the four middle schools, where a presentation is given and feedback requested; a community survey in March/April following the community meetings; and board of education consideration and a decision in April/May 2025.

President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Board members present were Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, and Wilson; Dr. Philippart was absent. The Board also recognized the Troy School District Communications Department for receiving 15 Michigan School Public Relations Association (MSPRA) awards, the most the team has ever earned: three Awards of Excellence and twelve Awards of Merit. Team members named were Melissa Verduyn, Thomas Butcher, Adam Burns, Linda Alfonso, Patrice Rowbal, and Alison Hendry. The Awards of Excellence were for Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (the Elevating Voices: In Comfortably Uncomfortable Conversations podcast), Marketing Materials (Early College with LTU), and Special Purpose (Coffee with the Superintendent). The awards were received in October, with formal recognition to follow at the MSPRA conference in March.

Consent Agenda: It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Haupt to approve items A through D: minutes of the October 1, 2024 Board Workshop; minutes of the October 15, 2024 Board meeting; the Treasurer's Report for September 2024; and rescheduling the January 7, 2025 Board Workshop to January 14, 2025. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Supplemental documentation for Troy School District RFP 2425-03 explaining why the Floor Polishing category received only a single bid. The memo notes floor polishing is a niche category, that five qualified contractors were contacted and invited to bid, and that the small scope, heavy existing bid activity in metro Detroit, and the required work window limited interest. It recommends Diamond Shine, which has performed this work for the district several times over the past four years at comparable per-square-foot pricing, and notes the polishing is needed at the Athens concessions stand in February to stay ahead of the spring sports season.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A supplemental justification memo (agenda item 3.c) for Troy School District RFP 2425-03, Flooring Replacement & Polishing, addressing the lone bidder in the Floor Polishing category.

Why only one bid
- Floor polishing tends to be a niche category; five contractors that perform this work were contacted and invited to bid
- The specified polishing scope is small and generated limited interest
- Heavy existing bid work in the metro Detroit area and the narrow required work window further reduced participation

Recommendation and rationale
- Diamond Shine is recommended; it has been awarded and performed this category of work for Troy School District several times over the past four years and is described as a good fit for the size and time of year specified
- Its bid pricing is comparable on a square-foot basis with previous years
- Extending the RFP timeline is judged unlikely to attract additional bidders

Timing
- The district intends to perform the floor polishing at the Athens concessions stand in February; delay would jeopardize completing that portion before the spring sports season

Purpose
Provides the Board the lone-bidder justification supporting acceptance of the single floor-polishing bid submitted under RFP 2425-03.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Supplemental documentation prepared for the Troy School District's RFP 2425-03, the Flooring Replacement & Polishing RFP, and designated agenda item 3.c. Its purpose is to justify accepting a single (lone) bid in the Floor Polishing category. The memo explains that the floor-polishing category received only one bid because it tends to be a niche category: five contractors that perform this type of work were contacted and invited to bid on the RFP.

According to the memo, the size of the district's polishing work as specified in the RFP documents is small and did not generate much interest, a situation compounded by the amount of bid work currently available in the metro Detroit area and by the narrow window of time in which the district needs the work performed.

The memo recommends Diamond Shine, stating that the firm has been awarded and has performed this category of work for Troy School District several times over the past four years and seems to be a good fit for the size and time of year the district specifies. It notes the bid pricing is comparative on a square-foot basis with previous years, and that the district is not likely to achieve additional bidders by extending the RFP bid timeline. Finally, it explains the practical driver of the schedule: the district wants to perform the floor polishing at the Athens concessions stand in February, and delaying would put that portion of the project in jeopardy of not being completed prior to the spring sports season. The document supports the award recommendation reflected in the accompanying bid tabulation.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A slide deck presenting the Attendance Area Review Committee (AARC) proposal to the Troy Board of Education, part of the district's periodic review of enrollment patterns across its four middle schools. It documents enrollment “splits” as students change school levels (notably a double split at Troy Union) and disparate middle-school enrollment ranging from 590 to 870 students, and argues for an optimal middle-school size near 750 built around 125-student learning communities. The 25-member committee, formed in 2024 with demographers Plante Moran, met five times in fall 2024; the presentation outlines a four-phase process moving toward a board recommendation in January and community listening sessions February through April 2025.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is: “Attendance Area Review Committee Proposal” presentation to the Troy Board of Education (District: Troy).

Background — why: TSD historically reviews enrollment patterns every 5–10 years; prior AARC groups convened in 2015 and 2018, and a 62-member Facilities Review Committee (2021/22) informed the 2022 bond proposal. Challenges include enrollment “splits” as students move between school levels — a double split at Troy Union and single splits at Smith, Baker, Wattles, and Hamilton — and uneven middle-school enrollment (590–870 per building). The new Smith Middle School was built for an optimal enrollment of 750; all four middle schools rank in Metro Parent’s top 6 in Michigan.

Optimal-size model: Learning community = 125 students; average class size 25; teachers teach 5 sections; two learning communities per grade (250 in grade 6); grades 6–8 = 750 students, flexible up to 900. Smaller schools bring more partial/shared staff, fewer course sections (e.g., only 2 sections of art), and higher costs; larger schools bring staffing overages and building congestion.

Process: Hired Plante Moran (demographers) for yearly and future enrollment projections. AARC formed in 2024 with 25 members (15 administrators, 10 community members); applications requested in September; met October 14 & 28, November 11 & 25, and December 9, 2024, with weekly cabinet discussions since August 2024. TSD directed the committee toward a four-middle-school future with balanced enrollment.

Phases: (1) Discovery; (2) Recommendation to the board in January; (3) Feedback — four listening sessions (one per middle school) plus a community survey, February–April; (4) Determination in April/May.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A presentation titled “Attendance Area Review Committee Proposal” delivered to the Troy Board of Education, laying out the rationale, committee work, and next steps for reviewing attendance-area and enrollment distribution across the district’s middle schools.

Background (why): The district has a historic practice of reviewing enrollment patterns and challenges every 5–10 years, with previous AARC groups in 2015 and 2018 and a Facilities Review Committee in 2021/22 (62 members, a 6-month process that created recommendations for the 2022 bond proposal, with staff, student, cabinet, and board feedback). Challenges to explore include enrollment “splits” when students transition from one school to the next (elementary to middle, or middle to high), where a student body splits to attend different feeder schools — a double split at Troy Union and single splits at Smith, Baker, Wattles, and Hamilton. Additional factors include middle-school ratios, enrollment ranging from 590 to 870 at each middle school building, enrollment projections, birth rate/students of the community, the new Smith Middle School (built for optimal enrollment of 750), and Metro Parent rankings placing all four middle schools in the top 6 in Michigan.

Optimal middle-school size: The district's ideal parameters set a learning community at 125 students, average class size 25, full-time teachers teaching 5 sections (5 x 25 = 125), two learning communities per grade level (250 in grade 6), for grades 6–8 totaling 750 students. Learning communities can flex up to 900 students as class size rises above 25, or below 750 as class size dips under 25 (raising costs). Benefits of optimal enrollment include more full-time elective staff, three lunch periods aligned to grade levels, and comfortably enrolled buildings. Smaller schools risk more part-time/shared staff, cultural impact, limited course availability (e.g., only 2 sections of art), higher costs from lower class sizes, staff split across content areas, and fewer students for extracurriculars such as jazz band, theatre, and yearbook. Larger schools risk staffing “overages” (e.g., more than a 1.0 orchestra teacher, teachers giving up prep periods), physical congestion in classrooms, hallways, and cafeterias, saturated clubs/athletics, and limited ability to support move-in families.

Process to date: The district hired Plante Moran as demographers for yearly and future enrollment projections. The AARC group formed in 2024 with 25 members — representation from each elementary and middle school, comprising 15 administrators and 10 community members — with applications requested in September and a 3-month process spanning meetings on October 14, October 28, November 11, November 25, and December 9, plus weekly cabinet discussions since August 2024. The committee found there are many ways to achieve the district’s goals, each with challenges; TSD directed the committee to focus on a four-middle-school future and how best to achieve a balanced distribution of enrollment. Feedback gave the district pause about better understanding community priorities and values — such as programmatic experience, community schools/location, in-school enrollment size, and bus ride duration.

Phases: Phase 1 Discovery (committee formed; research, analysis, planning; developing potential recommendations); Phase 2 Recommendation in January (committee provides the board options and the board decides whether to move forward); Phase 3 Feedback (February–April) with four listening sessions for families, one at each middle school, plus a community survey; and Phase 4 Determination (April/May), when TSD summarizes feedback and the board determines any future changes. The deck also references data on enrollment, grade cohorts, boundaries, birth rates, resident/non-resident/employee feeder paths, current maps, and demographic data.

From: Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D. To: Board of Education.

Order of business:
1. Election of an acting chairperson to conduct the meeting until a president is elected.

3. Election of President - nominations need not be seconded; four votes required for election.
4. Election of Vice President - same procedures.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This agenda memo, on Troy School District / Troy Board of Education letterhead, is from Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D., to the Board of Education, subject "Agenda Memo for the Organizational Meeting, January 21, 2025." It sets out the procedural sequence the board follows to reorganize its officers.

The order of business is: (1) Election of Acting Chairperson - the first order of business is to elect an acting chairperson who conducts the meeting until a president is elected. (2) Appointment of Temporary Secretary - the acting chairperson appoints Judy Holmes to act as temporary secretary until the board secretary is elected. (3) Election of President - the acting chairperson declares nominations in order; nominations need not be seconded, a motion and support are made to close nominations, and four votes are required for election. (4) Election of Vice President - the newly elected president declares nominations in order, following the same procedures as for president. (5) Election of a Secretary - the president declares nominations in order, following the same procedures. (6) Appointment of Treasurer - according to Board Policy the treasurer is appointed annually by the Board as a nonvoting officer; the assistant superintendent of business services has served as treasurer, and the superintendent recommends this procedure continue.

The memo is purely procedural, documenting the standing rules for the board's annual organizational reorganization rather than any substantive policy or expenditure.

Larger schools risk staffing "overages" (e.g., needing more than a 1.0 orchestra teacher), teachers giving up prep periods, classroom, hallway, and cafeteria congestion, saturated clubs and athletics, and limited ability to absorb move-in families.

Feedback gave the district pause on how to better understand and uphold community priorities and values such as programmatic experience, location/community schools, enrollment size, and bus-ride duration.

Minutes of a regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education (Troy, Michigan) held December 17, 2024 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. Vice President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, board members Alic, Hauff, Haupt, and Philippart were present; President Schmidt and Dr. Wilson were absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Montante, DiPilato, Griffor, Pagel, Burden, and Trudell. Approximately 75 members of the audience attended.

Recognition. The Board recognized Athens High School, selected to be honored by the American Red Cross for hosting community blood drives. Carmen Timm of the American Red Cross recognized Athens teachers Shawn DuFresne and Deanna Fakhouri and their students, who run blood drives to earn scholarship money; students recognized were Claire Kilbride, Maggie Ianev, Everett Marshall, Willow Bodendorfer, and Jack Appledorn.

Mission Moment. The Board recognized Troy High Colts who attended the Global Leadership Summit in Berlin, Germany the prior summer. Selected for leadership and character, the students travelled to the French Riviera, Switzerland, and Berlin to explore 'the Impact of Water on Society,' among 1,100 students worldwide; working in teams, they used design thinking to prototype solutions and deliver one-minute pitches to judges. Communications Instructor and Global Leadership Summit Adviser Harriet Clark recognized students Ashley Carron, Anusha Gupta, Ava Fleming, Jake Baker, Josie Lido, Katerina Zak, Kate Bestul, Vivian Edoff, Nicole Gherase, Laith Hermiz, Nainika Jasti, Keira McComb, Shreyan Maini, Maya Saad, Neel Nagappala, and Tia Tonelli.

Student Spotlight. The TSD Creative Guild spotlight honored Ryan Stasinski, a senior at Athens High School with a passion for sports; Thomas Butcher spoke about his work. Student representative reports were then given by Nurayda Albeez (International Academy-East), Kristian Vitanovich (Troy College and Career High School), Madie Miller (Troy High School, filling in for Adam McManus), and Diana D'Aloisio (Athens High School).

Consent Agenda. On a motion by Mr. Hauff, supported by Mr. Haupt, the Board resolved to approve items A, B, C, and D: minutes of the November 12, 2024 Board Workshop; minutes of the November 19, 2024 Board Meeting; the Treasurer's Report for October 2024; and Budget Amendment #1. The vote was Yes 5, No 0, with Schmidt and Wilson absent.

Business — Playground Equipment Purchase Phase 2. On a motion by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Alic, the Board awarded the bid for playground equipment and installation as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund: Sinclair Rec/GameTime (Contractor #1) $1,246,295.60 and Midstate Rec/Playworld (Contractor #2) $1,320,079.97, for a total of $2,566,375.57. The vote was Yes 5, No 0, with Schmidt and Wilson absent.

Business — Playground Site Work. On a motion by Dr. Philippart, supported by Mrs. Alic, the Board moved to award the bid for playground site work as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund; the first line item awarded was 'Sitework1' to Santoro Services for $874,537.00, covering the Costello, Hamilton, and Wattles sites. The extracted text truncates at this point, so the remaining site-work awards and the final vote on this item are not captured.

The pre-printed agenda structure also shows sections for Additions and Deletions, Public Communication, Personnel, Curriculum, Board Comments, and Adjournment; several of these were recorded as 'None' in the meeting.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A monthly Cash Position Report for the Troy School District for the period ended November 30, 2024, reconciling beginning cash, revenues received, expenditures, and ending cash across four fund groups: General (funds 101, 120, 122), Special Revenue (520, 529, 530, 531), Debt Service (315, 316, 320, 321), and Capital Projects (419, 423, 498, 499).

Beginning cash at October 31, 2024 totaled $227,551,355, composed of $33,367,764 (General), $11,494,085 (Special Revenue), $13,639,181 (Debt Service), and $169,050,325 (Capital Projects).

Revenues received during November totaled $24,689,958. State aid of $13,711,211 was received almost entirely in the General Fund ($13,035,251), with $675,960 to Special Revenue. Other receipts included federal grant revenue of $852,981 ($199,574 General; $653,408 Special Revenue), state grant revenue of $271,183, local revenue of $387,049, interest income of $843,744 (of which $743,937 in Capital Projects, $70,293 in the General Fund, and $29,513 in Debt Service), property tax revenue of $113,899, athletics revenue of $56,198, and an $8,453,693 interfund transfer into the General Fund.

Expenditures totaled $31,047,992, comprising accounts payable of $12,593,221 (including $8,471,104 in Capital Projects), payroll of $4,568,228, payroll tax and ORS (Office of Retirement Services) withholdings of $5,432,850, and an $8,453,693 transfer out of Capital Projects (matching the transfer into the General Fund).

Ending cash at November 30, 2024 totaled $221,193,321: General $42,694,870, Special Revenue $11,920,078, Debt Service $13,703,438, and Capital Projects $152,874,935. Overall cash fell by roughly $6.4 million for the month. The General Fund grew by about $9.3 million on the strength of state aid and the interfund transfer, while the Capital Projects funds declined roughly $16.2 million as bond-funded construction spending ($8.47 million in accounts payable plus the $8.45 million transfer) continued. Debt Service cash was essentially flat, rising modestly on interest and property-tax receipts. The report is unaudited and serves as the Board's monthly liquidity snapshot.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An unaudited Statement of Revenues and Expenditures for the Troy School District covering July 1, 2024 through November 30, 2024 - the first five months of fiscal year 2024-25 - presented as separate budget-to-actual schedules for the General Fund, the Consolidated Debt Service Funds, and several special revenue funds.

General Fund revenues carry an approved budget (as amended 12/17/24) of $192,509,567 against year-to-date actual of $54,092,233. State sources dominate the budget, but most state aid is received later in the year, so only about 22% is realized to date.

General Fund expenditures are budgeted at $194,936,368 with $56,900,642 actual. Instruction totals $122,727,387 budget / $33,598,921 actual, split among Basic Programs ($91,558,112 / $24,737,167), Added Needs ($30,085,945 / $8,602,142), and Adult Education ($1,083,330 / $259,612). Support Services total $71,247,680 / $23,105,453, including Pupil ($16,303,720 / $4,240,871), Instructional Staff ($12,964,602 / $3,798,842), General Administration ($2,505,398 / $882,907), School Administration ($10,176,228 / $3,321,969), Business Services ($2,402,724 / $671,601), Operations ($15,306,065 / $5,874,319), Pupil Transportation ($5,141,953 / $1,348,109), Central Services ($3,794,770 / $1,940,658), and Athletics/Other ($2,652,220 / $1,026,176). Community Services ($315,004 / $80,652), Debt Service ($478,500 / $115,617), and Outgoing Transfers ($167,797 / $0) round out spending. The General Fund shows a budgeted deficit of $2,426,801 and an actual year-to-date shortfall of $2,808,409.

The Consolidated Debt Service Funds report revenues of $31,930,500 budget / $16,225,010 actual (mostly local property taxes of $15,864,841) and expenditures of $31,709,530 / $5,146,915, of which interest is $5,146,265; scheduled principal of $21,415,000 had not yet been paid at mid-year, producing a year-to-date surplus of $11,078,095.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A candidate-information and voting-procedures booklet for the 2025 Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Board of Directors election, included in the Troy Board of Education's February 11, 2025 workshop materials.

Membership structure: MASB active membership comprises the boards of education of Michigan public school districts, divided into eight regions defined by intermediate school district (ISD) boundaries and into seven groups by pupil membership (Group I all intermediate districts; Group II 0-1,400 pupils; Group III 1,401-2,500; Group IV 2,501-5,000; Group V 5,001-11,000; Group VI 11,001-40,000; Group VII more than 40,000). Troy School District falls in Region 8, which consists of Macomb ISD, Oakland Schools, and Wayne RESA.

Board composition: The MASB Board of Directors has 23 members, including three at-large directors. Sixteen directors are elected from the eight regions (two per region) and one director each is elected from Groups V, VI, and VII. Under Article VIII, Section 6 of the MASB Bylaws, only one director may be elected or appointed from any one local or intermediate school board, and under Article VIII, Section 8, an unopposed nominee is declared elected without an election.

2025 seats: Eight seats are up for election - Regions 1 (two-year term), 3, 4, 6 (open seat, one-year term), 7, and 8 (open seat), plus Groups V and VI (three-year terms unless noted). Five were unopposed and returning without ballots: Kristen Cambensy (Marquette Area Public Schools, Region 1); Rick Dernberger (Zeeland Public Schools / Ottawa Area ISD, Region 3); John Tramontana (DeWitt Public Schools, Region 4); Stephen Hyer (Clarkston Community Schools, Group V); and Marc Siegler (Walled Lake Consolidated Schools, Group VI).

Contested candidates, with online balloting in Regions 6, 7, and 8:
- Region 6 (one-year term): TiAnna Harrison (Kalamazoo Public Schools, Kalamazoo County); Elizabeth O'Dell (St. Joseph County ISD, St. Joseph County).
- Region 7 (three-year term): Guillermo Z. Lopez (Lansing School District, Ingham County); Cory McLaughlin (Jefferson Schools, Monroe County); Jack Temsey (Eaton RESA, Eaton County).
- Region 8 (three-year term): Jason Babbage (Allen Park Public Schools, Wayne County); Anisha Hannah (Pontiac School District, Oakland County); Paul Kolin (Bloomfield Hills Schools, Oakland County); Roderick Means (Westwood Community School District, Wayne County); Randel Meisner (Fitzgerald Public Schools, Macomb County); Scott Wallace (Fraser Public Schools); Ursula (Wester) Rogers (Romulus Community Schools, Wayne County); Lisa Valerio-Nowc (Clintondale Community Schools, Macomb County).

Voting procedures: Each active member district received one ballot, emailed to the superintendent's secretary on record with MASB on Friday, January 24, 2025; ballots could not be forwarded. No local district or ISD funds may be used to campaign for any candidate. The booklet notes that incumbents are shown in bold and includes background statements from each candidate to help boards make informed decisions.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A resolution of the Troy School District Board of Education calling on Congress and the Michigan Legislature to fully and permanently fund the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). It notes that when IDEA passed in 1975 the federal government pledged to cover 40 percent of the average per-pupil cost of special education but currently funds only about 10.7 percent, forcing districts to reallocate money from other programs. The resolution specifically urges passage of the IDEA Full Funding Act (S.2217/H.R. 4519), which would create a 10-year mandatory path to full funding.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A formal board resolution urging the federal and state governments to fully and permanently fund the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA).

Key points
- IDEA, passed in 1975, carried a federal commitment to pay 40 percent of the average per-pupil expenditure for special education.
- That pledge has never been met; IDEA is currently funded at approximately 10.7 percent, leaving a gap of billions of dollars.
- When IDEA costs are not federally funded, Troy School District must reallocate money from other programs, which the resolution says harms academic opportunities for all students, not only those with disabilities.
- It cites that students across the U.S. lost nearly $600 billion from state disinvestment in the decade following the Great Recession.
- A placeholder ([XX] percent) is left in the text for the share of Troy students with disabilities.

Resolved
- Calls on Congress to immediately pass the IDEA Full Funding Act (S.2217/H.R. 4519), creating a 10-year mandatory path to fully fund IDEA.
- Calls on the state legislature to provide adequate, equitable, and sustainable funding increases to districts.

Purpose
To add the Board's voice to advocacy for closing the special-education funding gap and to press elected officials for reliable, full funding. Presented at the February 11, 2025 Board of Education Workshop.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A formal resolution presented to the Troy School District Board of Education titled 'A Resolution Calling for Full, Permanent Funding of IDEA.' The resolution builds its case through a series of whereas clauses: it frames public education as the cornerstone of democracy; notes that in the decade following the Great Recession students across the U.S. lost nearly $600 billion from state disinvestment in public schools; observes that both state and federal funding was already failing to meet student needs before the COVID-19 pandemic; and states that since the pandemic students have needed additional academic, social, emotional, and mental-health support through targeted programming, additional personnel, enhanced professional development, new technology, and critical facility updates. It cites research consistently showing that increased education funding positively affects academic performance, increases graduation rates, and improves future earnings.

The resolution's central financial argument concerns the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), passed in 1975. At that time the federal government committed to pay 40 percent of the average per-pupil expenditure for special education so that every child with a disability would have access to a high-quality education. That financial pledge has never been met and is currently funded at approximately 10.7 percent, leaving a gap of billions of dollars. A placeholder reading '[XX] percent' is left in the text for the proportion of Troy School District students with disabilities. The resolution states that when the federal government does not properly fund IDEA-required services, Troy must reallocate money from other programs, and that this underfunding has negatively affected the academic opportunities of all students for generations, not just those with disabilities.

The operative 'now, therefore, be it resolved' section makes two calls to action: first, that the Troy School District Board of Education calls on Congress to immediately pass the IDEA Full Funding Act (S.2217/H.R. 4519), which would create a 10-year mandatory path to fully fund IDEA; and second, that the Board calls on the state legislature to provide adequate, equitable, and sustainable funding increases to districts to mitigate the harm caused by decades of underfunded schools. The document was included in the materials for the Board of Education Workshop held February 11, 2025.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025, a reference document describing the district's middle school philosophy, goals, outcomes, program structure, and course offerings. The philosophy statement commits the middle schools to academic excellence and to being developmentally responsive to young adolescents' innate curiosity, desire to expand their environment, and need for recognition and achievement, supported by a research-based curriculum with effective assessment, a shared vision fostering respect for learning and diversity, and a cooperative partnership with parents and community.

Nine middle school goals are listed, covering developmentally appropriate programs; meeting the needs of a diverse student population; developing skills and knowledge in the core subject areas; helping students discover interests, aptitudes, and abilities; providing diversified cultural, social, civic, vocational, and recreational experiences; guidance services promoting self-esteem, independence, and responsible behavior; community partnerships; transition from elementary to high school; and modeling healthy lifestyles. The outcomes section describes preparing each student to become a self-directed learner, a quality worker, a positive communicator, a collaborative and cooperative contributor, and an involved and visionary citizen, each with specific sub-traits.

A three-year program overview specifies requirements by grade. In 6th grade, all students take five academic classes plus required Physical Education every other day (EOD); music students take Band, Orchestra, or Choir EOD, while non-music students take Art EOD. In 7th grade, all students take four academic classes plus required Health/Physical Education (half year) and Digital Applications 1.0 (half year); music students choose a full-year Concert Band, Chamber Orchestra, or Choir, while non-music students take a total of one full year of electives. In 8th grade, all students take four academic classes plus, for music students, a full-year Symphonic Band, Advanced Orchestra, or Choir with electives totaling two full-year classes; non-music students take one full year of electives. 'EOD' is defined as Every Other Day.

The guide then begins detailing individual courses. Grade 6 required courses include ELA 6 (full year), in which students study literature of various genres and informational text including literary nonfiction, deepening comprehension of complex texts, making inferences based on textual evidence, examining thematic and character development, understanding claims and evidence, and building academic vocabulary and independent choice reading; and Language Arts 6 (full year), in which students study three types of writing: narrative, informational, and argumentative. The extracted text is truncated partway through the Grade 6 course descriptions.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A board-update presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education in February 2025 by New Solutions K12 (NSK-12), titled 'Improving Outcomes and Equity for Students with Disabilities & Other Students Who Struggle.' The presentation states four project goals: develop an understanding of current practices related to special education and supporting all struggling students; explore alignment of current practice with best practices; identify opportunities to raise student achievement and improve work-life balance for teachers and staff; and craft a plan for implementing prioritized opportunities.

NSK-12 describes itself as an experienced team that has served over 300 districts in more than 30 states and is the lead partner for state departments of education in Louisiana, Connecticut, Maryland, Virginia, and Vermont, with an evidence-based, 'bold yet practical' approach drawn from former superintendents, special-education directors, principals, instructional coaches, and teachers. It highlights Nate Levenson, a former superintendent who closed the achievement gap in Arlington, MA, has consulted for over 15 years, and has authored 6 books and 50+ whitepapers and articles. The firm states its best practices have been recommended by the U.S. Department of Education and can produce dramatic gains, citing a 66% reduction in the achievement gap. Results from Louisiana are emphasized: early adopters had the highest growth rates for students with disabilities based on LEAP scores; all early adopters outpaced the state average growth for students with disabilities by at least two-fold, some by three-fold and one by five-fold; nearly two-thirds of high-growth districts had top growth two years in a row; and in one district the number of schools identified for low performance for students with disabilities dropped from 10 to 3.

The Phase 1 project plan has three stages: Kickoff & Engagement (assemble a guiding coalition, share research on best practices, gather data on current practices), Analysis (interviews and focus groups, analyze district data and compare to benchmarks, develop key findings), and Share Findings (present strengths and preliminary areas of opportunity, discuss with the guiding coalition, prioritize and plan for implementation).

The summary of commendations for Troy includes hardworking, dedicated, caring teachers; the faith and confidence of parents and community; a deep understanding of reading best practices, particularly at the elementary level; a well-defined and consistently implemented elementary Multi-Tiered System of Support (MTSS); and the ability to serve students with severe needs in-district. The summary of opportunities lists five priorities: (1) expand the reach of elementary reading specialists; (2) build general education teacher capacity, including ensuring students with mild-to-moderate disabilities work toward the same standards and curriculum (2A), expanding instructional coaching (2B), and better integrating Special Education, ELD, and General Education (2C); (3) create comprehensive, coherent elementary schedules with time for tier 1, tier 2, and intervention; (4) implement best-practice secondary interventions, including extra-time intervention from content-strong teachers (4A) and creating a sense of urgency for change (4B); and (5) further align what is 'loose' and what is 'tight' across schools. Later slides urge staff not to exclude students with disabilities from best-practice interventions and to group students by common area of need for more effective intervention.
